opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so for me the significance is really about showing that you can flip the script on how we think about noise in computing. For decades, the entire paradigm of digital computing has been about fighting thermal fluctuations — you pump in a lot of energy to keep your bits deterministic, to keep them far above the noise floor. And that's incredibly wasteful, especially when a huge fraction of what we actually want to do in modern AI is probabilistic anyway. We're sampling from distributions, we're doing generative modeling, we're doing Bayesian inference. So we spend enormous energy making things deterministic, and then we spend more energy using pseudorandom number generators to put the randomness back in. It's kind of absurd when you step back and look at it.

What the superconducting experiment demonstrates is that you can build a physical system whose natural dynamics — including its thermal fluctuations — actually *are* the computation. You engineer the energy landscape of the device so that when it equilibrates, or when it evolves under these stochastic dynamics, it's effectively sampling from the distribution you care about. The noise isn't a bug; it's the resource.

Superconducting circuits were a nice place to start because we came from the quantum computing world, and we know how to design and control those systems really precisely. You get these very clean, well-characterized degrees of freedom, low dissipation, and you can tune couplings and potentials with a lot of control. So it was a good testbed to prove out the core physics — that you can get programmable, controllable stochastic dynamics out of hardware and use it as a computational primitive.

But to be clear, the bigger picture is not "everyone needs a dilution refrigerator." The point was a proof of principle. The longer-term path is bringing these ideas to room-temperature, scalable hardware — things that can be manufactured in standard processes — so that you can get orders of magnitude better energy efficiency for probabilistic AI workloads. If you think about where the scaling of AI is going, energy is becoming the binding constraint. So finding a physics-first approach, where you're matching the hardware to the actual mathematical structure of the algorithms, I think that's one of the most important things we can be doing right now.

So in a sense, the experiment is the first step in showing that thermodynamic computing isn't just a theoretical curiosity — it's something you can actually build, measure, and program. And that opens up a whole new branch of the tech tree.

r002.rationale: It says the longer-term path could deliver “orders of magnitude better energy efficiency” for probabilistic AI workloads, conveying many orders of magnitude greater efficiency than digital computing in context.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so for me the significance is really that we've shown the first end-to-end demonstration that you can take the physics of a system, in this case a superconducting circuit at cryogenic temperatures, and use its natural thermodynamic evolution to do a useful computation, specifically probabilistic computation, drawing samples from a distribution and doing things like matrix inversion through the physics itself rather than through a sequence of digital arithmetic steps.

And the reason that matters is that if you look at where AI is going, so much of the compute is fundamentally about sampling and about linear algebra. Diffusion models are sampling. Bayesian inference is sampling. A lot of optimization is really just noisy dynamics finding a low-energy state. And right now we emulate all of that noise and all of that stochasticity on deterministic digital hardware, which is incredibly wasteful. You're spending enormous amounts of energy generating pseudo-random numbers and doing floating point operations to simulate something that nature just gives you for free.

So the bet behind thermodynamic computing, and the bet behind Extropic, is that instead of fighting the noise, you embrace it. You build a physical system whose equilibrium distribution is the distribution you care about, you let it thermalize, and you read out the samples. The superconducting experiment was basically the proof of principle that this isn't just a nice theoretical story. We built the device, we coupled the degrees of freedom the way the math says you should, we let the system relax, and the statistics came out matching what the theory predicts. That closes the loop between the abstract framework of thermodynamic computation and a real piece of hardware you can measure.

I'd also say it's significant as a stepping stone rather than as an endpoint. Superconducting circuits are a beautiful platform for validating the physics because they're extremely low noise and very well understood, but you're not going to scale them to billions of units in a data center at four Kelvin. What the experiment lets us do is de-risk the approach, understand the scaling of things like energy per sample and precision, and then carry those learnings over to room-temperature, semiconductor-based versions that can actually be manufactured at scale. So it's the moment where the idea went from a paper to something you could hold in your hand, and that's a big psychological and technical milestone for the whole program.

r001.rationale: The response calls the experiment a proof of principle and discusses energy efficiency, but does not characterize this computer as about as energy-efficient as Verdon can imagine building one.

r002.rationale: It says digital hardware wastes energy and nature provides noise for free, but does not state that thermodynamic computing can be many orders of magnitude more energy-efficient.

astra-6.text:
I think the significance is that it gives us a way to test a different relationship between physics and computation. Usually, we engineer a computer to suppress thermal fluctuations so that it behaves as a reliable digital machine. In thermodynamic computing, we ask whether those fluctuations, together with the dynamics of the system, can actually do useful computational work.

The superconducting experiment is a way of making that question concrete: can we control a physical system so that its natural evolution produces a useful computational outcome? For something like sampling, randomness is part of what you want, so there’s an opportunity to use the physics directly.

But I’d distinguish demonstrating that principle from demonstrating a practical advantage. You still have to account for control, readout, refrigeration, and how the system scales. To me, the exciting part is opening an experimental route to computation where thermodynamics is an active resource.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using physical dynamics and thermal fluctuations for computation, but does not characterize the experiment as about as energy-efficient as Verdon can imagine building one.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that thermodynamic computing can be many orders of magnitude more energy-efficient than digital computing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the significance is that we can start treating thermodynamics as a computational resource. In conventional computing, we spend a great deal of effort suppressing fluctuations so that each operation behaves deterministically. Here, the idea is to engineer a physical system whose fluctuations and relaxation actually help perform the computation.

For probabilistic machine learning, that’s a natural fit: you often want samples from a distribution, rather than a single deterministic answer. If you can encode the relevant distribution in the physics, you can let the system evolve and sample its state.

I’d distinguish that promise from what one experiment establishes, though. A demonstration is a step toward testing this computing paradigm; it doesn’t by itself establish a useful advantage at scale. The interesting questions are whether you can make these systems programmable, couple enough elements together, and retain an advantage once you account for control, readout, and refrigeration.

r001.rationale: The response describes using thermodynamics and fluctuations for computation, but does not characterize the superconducting computer’s energy efficiency.

r002.rationale: The response makes no comparison of thermodynamic and digital computing energy use, or claim of many orders of magnitude in efficiency.
